stemMd:
In each of the last five years the grape harvest in the Calder valley has been judged of unusually high quality. Yet in each of those years rainfall in the valley was far below its long-term average, and growers there are forbidden by law to irrigate their vines.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the quality of the Calder valley harvests?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Wine made from Calder valley grapes has sold at higher prices, and won more awards, in each of the last five years than in earlier years.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Growers in the Calder valley have expanded their planted area in each of the last five years, mostly by planting young vines on former grazing land.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The prohibition on irrigation in the Calder valley has been in force for more than forty years and is strictly enforced by regular inspections.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Neighbouring valleys, where irrigation is permitted, also reported harvests of unusually high quality in each of the last five years.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Water-stressed vines produce smaller berries, and the compounds that determine a grape's quality are concentrated in the skin rather than in the juice.

explanationMd:
The puzzle assumes something the stimulus never states: that less water must mean worse grapes. An explanation is any fact that breaks that assumption and shows how the drought could have *produced* the quality rather than merely coexisting with it.

The choice describing how a water-stressed vine behaves supplies the mechanism in two steps.

1. Water shortage makes the berries smaller.
2. The quality compounds sit in the skin, not the juice.

A smaller berry has a higher ratio of skin to juice, because volume falls faster than surface area as a sphere shrinks. So the same quality compounds are dissolved in less liquid, and what reaches the press is more concentrated. The drought is not something the harvest survived; it is the reason the harvest was good. That is a complete explanation, and it is the only choice that offers one.

Use this test on every candidate: *can I state, in one sentence, how this fact leads to high-quality grapes in a dry valley?*

- The choice about expanded planted area: more land planted explains more grapes, not better ones, and young vines on former grazing land are not a usual source of a valley's best fruit. Quantity and quality are different variables, and the stimulus is about quality.
- The choice about neighbouring, irrigated valleys also doing well: if irrigated valleys did equally well, the puzzle only deepens, since it suggests something else entirely was responsible and leaves the Calder case unexplained.
- The choice about the forty-year-old, strictly enforced irrigation ban: a rule that old is a constant. A constant cannot explain something that is said to be unusual in the last five years; whatever explains a change must itself have changed or must interact with what changed.
- The choice about higher wine prices and more awards: both are consequences of high quality, or at most evidence of it. Naming a downstream effect is not explaining the cause.

That third check — *is this fact constant across the period the puzzle covers?* — is worth keeping. It disposes of a distractor on a great many explanation questions.

distractorRationale.b: Expanding the planted area bears on how much fruit is harvested, not on how good it is, and if anything planting young vines on former grazing land would be expected to dilute average quality, since young vines are not usually the source of a valley's best fruit. The choice trades on a general impression of prosperity rather than on any route to quality.
distractorRationale.d: This makes the situation harder to explain rather than easier. If valleys that could irrigate did just as well, then something other than water management drove the run of good years, and the specific puzzle, how an unirrigated valley thrived in drought, is left exactly where it was.
distractorRationale.c: A rule in force, and enforced, for over forty years has been constant throughout the five unusual years and through all the ordinary years before them, so it cannot account for what is distinctive about this period. Any fact that did not change cannot by itself explain a change.
distractorRationale.a: Higher prices and more awards are downstream of quality: buyers pay more and judges award more because the wine is good. Citing those reactions restates the phenomenon in economic and critical terms instead of identifying the agronomic conditions that produced it, which is what the question asks for.

accessibilityText: A short puzzle. The Calder valley's grape harvest has been judged unusually high in quality for five consecutive years, even though rainfall was far below average in each of those years and irrigation is prohibited there. The question asks which statement most helps to explain the harvest quality. Five answer choices, labelled A through E. No notation, tables or figures appear; the explanation refers qualitatively to the ratio of a berry's skin to its juice.

provenance.notes: Original stimulus and choices. Explanation item in which the apparent obstacle (water shortage) is itself the cause, via a mechanism supplied only by the key. The Calder valley is an invented place. Not derived from any published LSAT item.

review.author: lsat-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The paradox is high quality despite drought and no irrigation. The choice stating that water-stressed vines produce smaller berries and that quality compounds are concentrated in the skin explains it: smaller berries mean more skin relative to juice, so dryness raises quality. Higher prices/awards restate quality; expansion onto grazing land with young vines does not link to dryness; the long-standing ban adds nothing new; irrigated neighbours also doing well points away from dryness as the cause and does not explain Calder's result. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch2-run1) reached the same answer: The puzzle is high quality despite dry years with no irrigation. The choice about water-stressed vines giving smaller berries, with the quality compounds held in the skin, explains how drought itself raises quality: more skin relative to juice. The higher-prices choice restates the high quality without explaining it. The young-vines and forty-year-ban choices do not link to quality. The neighbouring-valleys choice hints at a regional cause but does not say what it is, so it explains nothing.]

review.notes: Author solved the item and then tried to construct an explanatory route from each other choice to high grape quality; the choice about planted area addresses quantity, the choice about irrigated neighbours deepens the puzzle, the choice about the irrigation ban is constant across the period and the choice about wine prices is an effect rather than a cause. Only the choice about water-stressed vines and berry skins states a mechanism. Awaiting blind independent solve.
